tagline.text: An 18th-century coral-stone Baroque church on the Loboc River, with a three-storey convent museum

location.label: Location
location.text: Poblacion, Loboc, Bohol, on the bank of the Loboc River (about 24km from Tagbilaran)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (half a day combined with a Loboc River cruise)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,500 (per person, round-trip transport from Tagbilaran and lunch)

children.text: Loboc Church is the parish church of San Pedro Apostol, a Baroque coral-stone building completed in 1734. It has ceiling paintings, an organ loft and a three-storey convent museum, and it reopened in May 2021 after restoration of the damage from the 2013 earthquake.

Loboc Church is formally the San Pedro Apostol Parish Church, and since May 2021 it has also been called the Diocesan Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Extremadura. It stands in the Poblacion of Loboc in central Bohol, right above the Loboc River, and according to most sources it lies about
24km

from Tagbilaran. Because it is within walking distance of the pier for the Loboc River cruise, a staple of any Bohol trip, many travelers drop by before or after the floating buffet cruise. The building was declared a National Historical Landmark on December 12, 1998, and a National Cultural Treasure on July 31, 2001.

Its history goes back to late 1596. The Jesuit Fr. Juan de Torres founded a second mission station at Loboc, after Baclayon, and the first church was a wooden building at Calvario (Sawang) dedicated to the Archangel St. Michael. Loboc became a parish in 1602, and because Baclayon suffered frequent pirate raids and Loboc had a better position, the Jesuits made it their mission center. In 1605 a boarding school for boys, the Seminario de los Indios, opened. After a fire destroyed the wooden church in 1638 it was rebuilt, a larger church was built in 1670 on the site of today's convent, and the present coral-stone church was completed and consecrated in 1734. After the Jesuits were expelled in 1768, the Augustinian Recollects took over the parish that November.

The style is Baroque in coral stone, with a cruciform plan and a pyramidal roof over the crossing. The outer walls still carry Jesuit insignia and winged angel-head motifs. The inner façade, built in 1734, has pilasters, capitals, blind niches and volutes, and is said to be modeled on San Ignacio Church in Intramuros, Manila. In front of it is a neoclassical portico added by Fr. Aquilino Bon in 1863–1866, with niches for Saints Peter and Paul and a wooden relief of a papal tiara over crossed keys. The floor was replaced with cement tiles in 1895 and raised once in 1969 because of flooding.

What makes this church special is that the façade and part of the bell tower collapsed in the magnitude 7.2 Bohol earthquake of October 15, 2013, and it returned after a long restoration. The National Museum led the work, which went ahead after a groundbreaking in late 2017, and the church was turned over to the diocese and reopened on the same day, May 16, 2021. For a while after the quake, Mass was held in an alternate church that opened in October 2014. Today you can see the restored ceiling paintings, the organ loft, the three-storey convent museum and the riverside bell tower in a single visit. Keep in mind that this is both a heritage site and a church still used by parishioners, so interior access can be limited depending on Mass times and events.

blocks.title: Ceiling paintings and the Our Lady of Guadalupe mural

children.text: The ceiling of the nave carries paintings made from May 1926 to July 1927 by Canuto Ávila and his sons, retouched once in 1995. At the center is a 1930 mural of Our Lady of Guadalupe by Max Aya-ay, which depicts the story of the Virgin saving Loboc from floods. The colors, seen again after the restoration, are the church's biggest attraction.

blocks.title: The main altar and five retablos

children.text: The church has five retablos (altarpieces) in all. The main retablo is centered on the patron saint, St. Peter, with St. Paul above and Our Lady of Guadalupe below, along with statues of St. Lucy and St. Francis Xavier. Behind it, a stucco relief of Ignatius of Loyola and Francis Xavier from the earlier Jesuit altarpiece is said to be hidden.

A cantilevered organ loft above the entrance holds a large pipe organ. It is said to be connected to Fr. Diego Cera, who built the Las Piñas Bamboo Organ, but this is not confirmed by solid records. Look up and take in the ceiling paintings and the loft structure together.

The convent beside the church was built around 1854 as the main Jesuit residence in Bohol, a three-storey stone house (bahay na bato) with thick walls and a two-storey gallery. The Loboc Museum on the third floor displays items such as an 1786 silver missal and an 18th-century wooden Santo Niño. Opening hours and fees may change, so check locally.

The four-storey bell tower, set apart from the main building near the riverbank, has seven bells. The oldest dates from 1863 and the largest from 1937, named for Fr. Cayetano Bastes. It also has a wooden matraca (1899), used when the bells are silenced during the Easter Triduum, and an 1893 clock by the Altonaga company.

On the left of the façade is a hexagonal chapel built by Fr. Aquilino Bon in 1867–1868. It originally received bodies for funerals and is now used as an adoration chapel. Unlike the busy outdoors, many people pray quietly here, so be respectful when taking photos.

blocks.title: Tomb of the Jesuit Fr. Alonso de Humanes

children.text: Near the altar on the right (Epistle) side are the tombs of Recollect priests and the place where the Jesuit Fr. Alonso de Humanes was buried. His remains were later moved to Intramuros, but a story says a fire stopped in front of his tomb, and pilgrims still light candles there. Take it lightly, knowing it is a legend.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: The church and a Loboc River cruise

children.text: Leave Tagbilaran for Loboc. It takes about 30 minutes by car and longer by public transport.
See the façade and bell tower from the plaza first, then go inside when no Mass is under way to look at the ceiling paintings and altars.
Visit the museum on the third floor of the convent (check opening hours locally).
Board a Loboc River cruise at the pier close to the church.
Finish the cruise, have lunch and head to your next stop.
Cruise boats are generally said to leave once they fill up, roughly between 10 AM and 1 PM, so confirm the exact time at the pier.

items.title: Central Bohol full-day route
items.subtitle: A day linking church, forest and tarsiers

children.text: Leave Tagbilaran and either see Baclayon Church first or go straight to Loboc.
Look around Loboc Church and its museum.
Have lunch on the Loboc River cruise.
Pass through the Bilar Man-Made Forest, taking it in from the car window.
Quietly watch the tarsiers at the Tarsier Sanctuary.
Return to Tagbilaran or Panglao.
A full-day route is easiest with a rental car or a car with a driver. You can change the order to fit Mass times and the cruise schedule.
Direct flights run from Manila Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Bohol-Panglao International Airport (TAG). Check flight times, airlines and schedules when you book.
You can also go via Cebu and take a ferry to Tagbilaran, but ferry schedules and travel times differ by operator, so check locally.

items.title: From the airport or Tagbilaran to Loboc

children.text: From Tagbilaran, Loboc is about
24km
away according to sources, and the trip is said to take about
30 minutes
by car or motorcycle.
From the Panglao side you pass through Tagbilaran, so it takes longer. The most common approach is to rent a car with a driver for the day and combine Loboc with other sights.
A jeepney (or van) from the Dao terminal in Tagbilaran to Loboc takes about
40–50 minutes
according to sources. Check fares and operating hours locally.
The last ride back may leave early, so if you plan to stay until late afternoon, decide how you will return first.
The church, convent and bell tower are all in the same grounds and can be seen on foot. The cruise pier is also said to be within walking distance of the church.
To reach the Bilar forest or the Tarsier Sanctuary you can hire a tricycle or motorcycle. Fares need to be negotiated, so agree on one before you ride.

Bohol is relatively dry from December to May, which is good for visiting the church and taking the Loboc River cruise. The inside of the church is fairly cool, but the plaza and steps get hot at midday, so bring a hat.

This is still a working parish church, so tourist access may be limited during Sunday Mass. A weekly listing for August 2025 shows several Sunday Masses from early morning to evening, so check exact Mass times with the parish office or its Facebook page. The riverside is busiest from about 9:30 AM to 1:30 PM, so early morning or late afternoon is quieter.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Best for the church and the cruise, but crowded at year end with many Masses and events
Visit early in the morning and rest in the shade of the church at midday
Heavy rain can make the cruise difficult, so plan around the indoor museum

Loboc is a rural town, so most travelers stay in Tagbilaran or Panglao and visit as a day trip. There are small lodgings and resorts along the Loboc River, so staying a night is an option if you want to add the cruise and a firefly tour. Names and rates change often, so check recent reviews on a booking site.

The most typical meal is the buffet on the Loboc River cruise, with Filipino dishes and live folk music; one source describes the meal as less about the food than about enjoying the river scenery and music. The town has simple restaurants and shops, so have lunch on the cruise or at a local eatery, and bring cash because ATMs in town are few.
The church can be closed to visitors during Sunday Mass and events, so a weekday visit around midday is easiest.
Dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered inside, and avoid taking photos in front of people at Mass or in prayer.
You will spend a long time looking up at the ceiling paintings, so take it slowly to avoid a stiff neck.
The convent museum is up stairs to the third floor, so check ahead if mobility is a concern.
Cruise seats fill early in the December–April peak season, so ask whether to reserve.
Bring plenty of cash, and consider helping with upkeep through the donation box or at the museum.
Loboc Church is a parish church still used by worshippers and a heritage building restored after the earthquake. Keep quiet during Mass and prayer and follow staff instructions and access limits.
Entrance fees, museum hours and Mass times differ by source, and some are unconfirmed. Check locally or with the parish announcements.
This is a restored building, so do not touch the walls, altars or ceiling paintings, and avoid using flash.
Check prices and itineraries first before agreeing with touts around the riverside pier.
The riverside steps can be slippery in the rain, and cruises may be cancelled.
This information reflects what could be verified as of 2026, and fees and hours may change. Check the latest announcements.
The
Loboc River
cruise, which leaves from a pier within walking distance of the church, is the signature Bohol itinerary.
Baclayon Church
, a leading coral-stone church of Bohol, shares its Jesuit history with Loboc Church. It is worth seeing the two together.
The
Bilar Man-Made Forest
lies on the road running east from Loboc, where mahogany trees line the road like a tunnel.
At the
Tarsier Sanctuary
you can see tarsiers. Avoid noise and flash, and observe quietly.
Bohol's gateway city,
Tagbilaran City
, is the starting point for visiting Loboc and has plenty of lodging and restaurants.
